title: Koi pond — 12 fish: skin ulcers and flashing after a pond top-up
presentation: A garden pond of twelve koi. Four fish have raised red ulcers on the flank, all are rubbing against the pond walls, two sit apart with clamped fins, and one has died. The pond was topped up from the mains a fortnight ago and two new fish were added.

stages.title: Assess the pond and the fish
stages.briefing: Affected fish: focal raised ulcers with reddened margins on the flanks, scale loss, one with a frayed caudal fin. All fish flashing and rubbing. Two lethargic with clamped fins at the surface. One death. Pond: 3,000 litres, no biological filter maturation after a filter clean three weeks ago, topped up 30% from the mains without dechlorination, two new koi added without quarantine, water temperature 14°C and rising.

options.label: Flashing and rubbing in every fish, not only the ulcerated ones
options.detail: Whole-pond irritation — parasites or water quality

options.label: A 30% mains top-up with no dechlorination after a filter clean
options.detail: Two insults to gill and skin at once

options.label: Focal ulcers with reddened margins in four fish
options.detail: Bacterial invasion of damaged skin

options.label: Rising water temperature from 14°C
options.detail: Relevant to disease dynamics, but not a clinical finding

options.label: Frayed caudal fin in one fish
options.detail: Non-specific damage

stages.explanation: The distinction that matters is between what affects every fish and what affects four: whole-pond flashing points at water quality or an ectoparasite, while focal ulcers are where bacteria have got into damaged skin. A filter clean followed by an undechlorinated top-up is a classic double insult — the biology gets killed twice.

stages.title: Choose the tests
stages.briefing: You are at the pond with a microscope, water test kit and the ability to net and sample fish.

options.label: Full water chemistry — ammonia, nitrite, nitrate, pH, chlorine, oxygen, temperature
options.detail: In fish medicine the water is the patient

options.label: Skin and mucus scrape wet mounts examined immediately
options.detail: Motile ectoparasites die and disappear on a stored slide

options.label: Gill biopsy wet mount
options.detail: The organ that shows both parasites and water damage

options.label: Bacterial culture and sensitivity from the leading edge of an ulcer
options.detail: Names the invader and picks the drug

options.label: Post-mortem of the dead fish including kidney and spleen
options.detail: Systemic spread, and a second sampling opportunity

options.label: Koi herpesvirus PCR as the only investigation
options.detail: A notifiable consideration at rising temperatures, but it will not explain flashing and ulcers alone

options.label: Faecal parasitology as a priority
options.detail: Not how skin and gill disease is diagnosed

stages.explanation: Water chemistry comes first because in aquatic medicine the environment is part of the patient, and chlorine from an undechlorinated top-up would explain the gill damage that let everything else in. Scrapes and gill biopsies have to be read within minutes — the organisms you are looking for stop moving and become invisible.

stages.title: Interpret the results
stages.briefing: Water: ammonia 0.6 mg/L, nitrite 0.35 mg/L, nitrate 10 mg/L, pH 8.1, free chlorine 0.1 mg/L, dissolved oxygen 8 mg/L, temperature 15°C. Skin scrape: numerous Ichthyobodo and moderate Trichodina; no Argulus or Lernaea. Gill biopsy: epithelial hyperplasia with the same protozoa. Ulcer culture: Aeromonas salmonicida, sensitive to trimethoprim-sulfonamide and florfenicol, resistant to oxytetracycline. Post-mortem: pale kidney and spleen with the same organism cultured. Koi herpesvirus PCR negative.
stages.prompt: Which conclusions do these results support?

options.label: Ectoparasitic infestation on gill and skin
options.detail: Ichthyobodo and Trichodina on both sites

options.label: Immature filtration is producing ammonia and nitrite toxicity
options.detail: Ammonia 0.6 mg/L with nitrite 0.35 mg/L after a filter clean

options.label: Secondary Aeromonas salmonicida ulcer disease with systemic spread
options.detail: Same organism from ulcer, kidney and spleen

options.label: Oxytetracycline would be the wrong antibiotic
options.detail: The isolate is resistant to it

options.label: Koi herpesvirus is the primary problem
options.detail: PCR negative

options.label: Low dissolved oxygen is driving the outbreak
options.detail: Oxygen at 8 mg/L is adequate

stages.explanation: This is a three-layer problem and the layers have to be treated in order: the water is toxic, the parasites are stripping the skin and gills, and the bacteria are exploiting the damage. Treating the bacterium alone in bad water fails; killing the parasites in ammoniated water stresses the fish further. Excluding koi herpesvirus also settles a notification question at a rising water temperature.

stages.title: Commit to a diagnosis
stages.briefing: Ammonia 0.6 mg/L and nitrite 0.35 mg/L after a filter clean, Ichthyobodo and Trichodina on skin and gill, Aeromonas salmonicida from ulcer, kidney and spleen, resistant to oxytetracycline, KHV negative.

options.label: Ectoparasitism with secondary Aeromonas ulcer disease on a background of ammonia and nitrite toxicity
options.detail: All three layers, in the order they must be fixed

options.label: Koi herpesvirus infection
options.detail: PCR negative

options.label: Primary bacterial ulcer disease alone
options.detail: Ignores the parasites and the water chemistry that caused it

options.label: Chlorine gill burn as the sole diagnosis
options.detail: A contributing insult, but it does not explain the parasites or the ulcers

options.label: Spring viraemia of carp
options.detail: Not supported by any result here

stages.explanation: Writing all three layers into the diagnosis produces the right sequence: partial water changes with dechlorination and filter recovery first, an appropriate antiparasitic second, and a sensitivity-guided antibiotic for the ulcerated fish — plus quarantine for future arrivals, which is how the parasites arrived.
